title: When the Building Burns

post.author: u/letter_cutter_edern
post.title: I cut names into headstones. Tonight a family sent me the correction they emailed us nine days ago. Our archive has never heard of it.

blocks.text: I'm Edern, a letter cutter at Trethowan Memorials. Our archive holds every memorial we have carved since 1971, and every order in progress. It lives on a computer that stays on day and night to hold data, like a clerk who never goes home. That kind of computer is called a server. Ours is rented from Bramhope Hosting, a company that keeps servers in its own buildings.

Bramhope's site has two buildings, 50 metres apart. Our server is in building A. Every night at 01:00 a program reads the whole archive, copies it to a second server in building B, and checks the copy is complete. A spare copy like that is called a backup.

Putting a backup back takes two steps: set up a fresh server, then load the copy onto it. Anything written after the copy was made is gone. That is called a restore. On the first Sunday of each month, Bramhope did a practice restore. It always passed. Nothing had ever burned.

Every Friday at 17:30 our office manager, Gaynor, saves the archive onto a small plug-in disk, a USB drive, and locks it in the office safe: our export. On Friday the 12th she was at a wedding, and nobody else makes it.

A plan for getting back to work after losing a whole site is called disaster recovery. Ours had two numbers. The first is how much recent work we could afford to lose: the RPO, short for recovery point objective. With a backup every night, ours was one day.
The second is how long until we are working again: the RTO, short for recovery time objective. Bramhope's contract said four hours, restoring from building B.

Before we cut, each family checks the wording. On Monday the 8th at 09:12, Mr Elkanah Spurdle's daughter emailed about his. We had spelt him ELKANA. "It ends in h," she wrote. Gaynor corrected the archive at 09:40. Every backup from Tuesday on carried the h to building B.
At 00:40 on Sunday the 14th, fire broke out in building A. Our server burned, so the 01:00 backup never ran. By 03:00 the fire had crossed to building B. Both copies were gone.
Our backup log: date, time, copied from, copied to, size in GB (gigabytes, a measure of data), practice restore.

Fri 05 Mar  17:30  server A  USB drive  6.8 GB  none
Sun 07 Mar  01:00  server A  server B   6.8 GB  passed 02:30
Fri 12 Mar  -      -         USB drive  -       not made
Sat 13 Mar  01:00  server A  server B   6.9 GB  none

On Tuesday at 15:40 the archive was back, on a new hosting company's server, from the USB drive of Friday the 5th, nine days before the fire. Our real RPO was 8 days 7 hours 10 minutes; our real RTO, 63 hours.
Gaynor retyped every change she had on paper. The correction came by email, and our email burned too.
Today, Wednesday, I cut his stone from the archive. Tonight, gilding late, I sent his daughter a photo at 22:50.
At 23:06 she sent back a picture of her own sent mail: Monday the 8th, 09:12, "It ends in h." The stone says ELKANA.
Every backup that knew about the h was in building B. What should we change?

blocks.label: bramhope_fire_night.png

diagram.aria: Saturday 23:00 to Sunday 04:00 at Bramhope's site. Our server in building A runs until the fire reaches it at 00:40, then is gone. The backup server in building B runs until 03:00, when the fire crosses to it. The 01:00 backup never runs. The USB drive in the office, holding the archive as it was on Friday the 5th at 17:30, is safe all night. Markers: fire in A at 00:40, the 01:00 backup due, fire reaches B at 03:00.

blocks.caption: The fire night, redrawn from Bramhope's notice. Building A burns from 00:40, so the 01:00 backup has no server to copy. Building B, 50 metres away, burns from 03:00 with every backup that held the h. The only copy left is the USB drive in our office safe, made on Friday the 5th, before the correction.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Two words you'll need. Big hosting companies split their sites into groups of buildings, each group with its own power and cooling, kilometres from the next. Each group is called an availability zone. A set of zones in one part of the world, far from any other set, is called a region. Now some questions. Where was each copy on the night, and what reached it? Which copies held the h? When had anyone last restored from the USB drive? And on a bad week, how old can your newest safe copy be?

replies.author: u/letter_cutter_edern
replies.text: The server was in A, every backup in B, the USB drive in our office safe in town. The h was on the live server from Monday 09:40, and in every backup from Tuesday the 9th to Saturday the 13th, all in B. Nobody had restored the USB drive before Tuesday; it loaded fine, it was just old. On a bad week, like this one, the newest safe copy is two Fridays back.

comments.author: u/every_hour_morfydd
comments.text: Nightly is the weak spot. A whole day between copies is a whole day you can lose, and most firms I know back up every hour now. Gaynor fixed the h at 09:40; with hourly backups it would have been copied by 10:00. Hourly backups would have saved the inscription. Same servers, same buildings, just a better schedule.

comments.author: u/two_disks_tybalt
comments.text: Disks wear out far more often than buildings burn. Put two disks inside the one server and write every change to both at the same moment. That's called a mirrored disk. If one disk dies, the other carries on and not a minute of work is lost. No waiting for 01:00, ever.

reply.prompt: Bramhope is rebuilding, and we have to decide where the archive lives now. What should Trethowan Memorials change before the next fire? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Back up every hour instead of every night, so a copy is never more than an hour behind.
options.part2: We moved to hourly backups to building B. In the sim's replay of the fortnight, the h reached B at 10:00 on Monday the 8th, and a fresh copy followed every hour until 00:00 on Sunday: 313 backups in B. At 00:40 building A burned, and at 03:00 building B burned with every one of them. The newest copy left was still the USB drive from Friday the 5th: an RPO of 8 days 7 hours 10 minutes, 15 changes lost, 63 hours until we were working again, and on Wednesday the stone said ELKANA. The copies were newer. They were in the same place.
options.senior: How often you back up sets how much you lose when the copies survive. Where they live decides whether they survive. Hourly copies to the building next door shrink the RPO for a failed disk or a bad edit, and change nothing for a fire that reaches both buildings: the RPO falls back to whatever copy is outside the fire.

options.text: Add a mirrored disk to the server, so a second copy is written with every change.
options.part2: We added a mirrored disk. In the sim's replay, every change, the h included, went onto both disks at the same moment, so a dead disk would have cost nothing. At 00:40 the fire took the server, and both disks were inside it. At 03:00 building B burned as before. The newest copy left was the USB drive from Friday the 5th: an RPO of 8 days 7 hours 10 minutes, 15 changes lost, 63 hours until we were working again, and ELKANA on the stone.
options.senior: A mirrored disk is a replica, not a backup. It protects against one disk failing, and it copies every change, mistakes and deletions included, the instant they happen. It sits in the same box as the original, so anything that reaches the server, a fire, a flood or a theft, takes both.

options.text: Rent a third building at the same site, so a third copy sits in a building of its own.
options.part2: Bramhope rented us building C, at the far end of the same site, and every nightly backup went to B and to C. In the sim's replay, the fire took A at 00:40 and B at 03:00, and kept spreading: it reached C at 04:10, and 13 backups burned there, 5 of them holding the h. Three copies, one site, one fire. The newest copy left was the USB drive from Friday the 5th: an RPO of 8 days 7 hours 10 minutes, 15 changes lost, 63 hours until we were working again, and ELKANA on the stone.
options.senior: More buildings on one site guard against a fault in one building: a failed power supply, a broken cooling unit. They share the fence, the fire crew, the power line and the flood plain, and a fire has already crossed from one to the next. Copies usually only count as separate if no single event can reach them all, which means kilometres, not metres.

options.text: Send each nightly backup to another region too, with a practice restore monthly.
options.part2: We kept building B for quick restores and added a nightly copy to another region, with a practice restore on the first Sunday of every month. In the sim's replay, the far copy failed from its first night, with no warning: a wrong password. The practice restore at 02:30 on Sunday the 7th found it, and it was fixed. From Monday the 8th every backup reached the region, and from Tuesday every one carried the h. At 00:40 A burned; at 03:00, B. The region's Saturday 01:00 copy was restored by 04:40: an RPO of 23 hours 40 minutes, no typed change lost, an RTO of 4 hours, and on Wednesday the stone said ELKANAH.
options.senior: A backup protects you only from disasters that can't reach it. Keep a near copy for everyday restores and a far copy in another region, which no single fire, flood or power cut is likely to reach together with the first. Then prove it: restore from the far copy on a schedule, time it, and write down the RTO you actually got. A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a plan.

sim.title: Run Trethowan's fortnight at Bramhope
sim.lede: You're Gaynor, replaying the fortnight a day at a time, from Monday 1 March, 00:00, to Wednesday 17 March, 09:00, when the stone is cut. The office types 3 changes each weekday, at 09:40, 11:20 and 14:50: 30 in the fortnight. The Spurdle correction is Monday the 8th at 09:40. Each backup copies the whole archive as it is at that moment, while the server in building A stands. Building B already holds the backup of Sunday 28 February, 01:00, and the office safe the export of Friday 26 February. Exports are Fridays at 17:30; Friday the 12th is missed unless you switch it on. The practice restore is Sunday the 7th at 02:30. Fire takes A at 00:40 on Sunday the 14th (or 02:00); if it spreads, B burns 2 hours 20 minutes later, and building C, if you rent it, 3 hours 30 minutes later. A copy to another region starts with a wrong password, so it fails with no warning until a practice restore finds it. Restoring from a surviving hosted copy takes 4 hours; from the USB drive, it took until Tuesday 15:40. Nothing is typed after the fire. The stone is cut from whatever was restored.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to Wednesday as built. Building B burns at 03:00 with 14 backups, 5 of them holding the h; the newest copy left is the USB drive of Fri 05 Mar 17:30; the RPO is 8 days 7 hours 10 minutes, 15 changes are lost, the RTO is 63 hours, and the stone says ELKANA SPURDLE. Switch the export of Friday the 12th on: 1 day 7 hours 10 minutes, and the h survives, by luck. Now try each reply. Hourly backups: 313 backups burn, the same loss. Mirrored disk: it burns with the server. Buildings B and C: C burns at 04:10. Building B and another region, with the practice restore: 23 hours 40 minutes, 4 hours, ELKANAH SPURDLE. Then switch the practice restore off: the far copy never arrived. Last, stop the fire spreading and see what building B was for.

explain.oneLine: Nothing failed the way the plan expected. The backups ran every night and passed every practice restore; they just lived 50 metres from the server they protected. One fire reached both, and the only copy outside it was a USB drive made before the family's correction, so the restored archive, and the stone, still said ELKANA.

steps.title: Two copies, one site.
steps.text: First, each night at 01:00 a program read the archive on the server in building A. Then it copied it to the backup server in building B. Then it checked the copy was complete. Every step worked, every night, and the monthly practice restore proved the copies could be loaded. What went wrong was not a step but the place: A and B shared one site, one fence and one fire. When A burned at 00:40, the 01:00 run had no server to read. When the fire crossed to B at 03:00, every backup from Tuesday to Saturday, each holding the h, burned too.

steps.title: Why the USB drive was nine days old.
steps.text: The only copy outside the site was Gaynor's Friday export. It is a backup too, made by hand: save the archive to the drive, lock it in the safe. A step done by one person is skipped when that person is away. Friday the 12th was missed, so the newest export was from Friday the 5th at 17:30, three days before the correction. Everything typed after that, 15 changes in five working days, had to come back from paper. The correction came by email, and the email had burned with the server.

steps.title: RPO and RTO, written and real.
steps.text: The RPO, recovery point objective, is how much recent work you can afford to lose: the gap between the last good copy and the disaster. The written one was a day, because backups ran nightly. The real one was 8 days 7 hours 10 minutes, because the nightly copies burned. The RTO, recovery time objective, is how long until you are working again. The written one was 4 hours, restoring from B. The real one was 63 hours: Sunday 00:40 to Tuesday 15:40, finding a new hosting company and loading the USB drive. Both numbers are only as true as the copy they assume will be there.

steps.title: Zones, regions, and what one disaster can reach.
steps.text: Large cloud companies build for this. An availability zone is one or more data centres with their own power, cooling and network, kilometres from the next zone, so a fire or a power cut in one usually stays in one. Keeping copies in two zones, called multi-AZ, protects you from losing one zone. A region is a group of zones in one part of the world, isolated from other regions, so a copy in another region survives even a disaster that takes a whole area. Two halls 50 metres apart are neither: they are one zone with two doors. A useful habit: count copies by the places a single event cannot reach together.

steps.title: A backup you have not restored is a hope.
steps.text: A copy can fail without anyone noticing: a wrong password, a full disk, a changed setting. The only proof is to restore it. First, load the copy onto a fresh server. Then open real records and check them. Then time it, and compare that time with the RTO you promised. Do it on a schedule, from the far copy too. In the replay, a far copy set up with a wrong password failed every night, with no warning, until the practice restore on Sunday the 7th found it. GitLab learned the same in 2017: on the night, it found that of five backup and copy methods, none was working reliably, and its main backup had been failing silently with nobody responsible for testing it.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next fire. The server in building A sends a nightly backup at 01:00 to the backup server in building B on the same site, kept for quick restores, and a second nightly copy to another region, far from the site. A practice restore from the far copy runs on the first Sunday of every month. The office's USB export on Fridays at 17:30 stays as a third place.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next fire. Building B stays for quick restores when only the server fails. A second nightly copy goes to another region, where no fire on Bramhope's site can reach it, and a practice restore from it each month proves it loads. In the sim's replay: the far copy's Saturday 01:00 backup restored by 04:40, an RPO of 23 hours 40 minutes, and ELKANAH on the stone.

fix.title: The fix: a far copy, and proof that it loads
fix.text: Keep the nightly backup to building B for everyday restores, and send a second copy of each one to another region, far enough that no single fire, flood or power cut is likely to reach both. On the first Sunday of every month, restore from the far copy onto a fresh server, open some real records, and write down how long it took: that is your real RTO. Check each morning that last night's copies arrived, so a silent failure lasts a day, not a month. Keep the Friday export as a third place, but stop relying on one person to make it. In the sim's replay: the practice restore on Sunday the 7th caught the far copy failing, and after the fire the archive was back by 04:40 with the h.

limits: A far copy costs money every month and takes longer to restore than one next door; restoring a whole archive from another region can take hours of copying before the first record opens.
It does nothing for a mistake. A wrong edit or a deleted folder is copied faithfully to every place by the next night, so you also need older copies kept for weeks, not only the newest.
The RPO is still up to a day. Work typed after the last nightly copy is lost even when the copy survives; if a day is too much, copy more often to the far place, not only to the near one.

Good
Bad
rows: Nightly backups, tested monthly; quick restores from B.
One fire takes A and B; the USB drive is 9 days old; ELKANA on the stone.
Up to an hour lost when only the server fails.
B still burns at 03:00: the same 15 changes lost, the same stone.
A dead disk costs no work at all.
Both disks are in A and burn at 00:40; mistakes are mirrored too.
Survives a fault inside one building.
The fire reaches C at 04:10; one site is still one fire.
Survives the site: 23 hours 40 minutes lost, back in 4 hours, the h kept.
Costs more; slower restores; still up to a day of typing lost.

explain.seniorTake: A backup is only as good as the disaster it can't be reached by. Decide what you are protecting against, a failed disk, a deleted folder, a burned building, a lost region, and make sure each has a copy outside its reach: a mirror for the disk, older copies for the mistake, another zone for the building, another region for the area. Write down the RPO and RTO you need, then measure the ones you have by restoring from the far copy on a schedule, because both numbers assume a copy that is actually there and actually loads. Hand-made copies, like a USB drive, depend on one person and tend to be skipped on the day they're needed. The protocol at Trethowan's ran perfectly every night; it was protecting against the wrong disaster.

realWorld.title: OVHcloud, Strasbourg, March 2021: one building, then the site
realWorld.text: OVHcloud's incident page for the site, in its update of 02:53 UTC on 10 March 2021: "We are currently facing a major incident in our DataCenter of Strasbourg with a fire declared in the building SBG2." "Firefighters were immediately on the scene but could not control the fire in SBG2." "The whole site has been isolated, which impacts all our services on SBG1, SBG2, SBG3 and SBG4." And its advice: "If your production is in Strasbourg, we recommend to activate your Disaster Recovery Plan."

realWorld.title: OVHcloud: the fire reached the next building
realWorld.text: The Register embedded the founder Octave Klaba's tweet of 10 March: "Fire destroyed SBG2. A part of SBG1 is destroyed. Firefighters are protecting SBG3." A backup kept in a neighbouring building on that site was within reach of the same fire, as Trethowan's was.

realWorld.title: AWS: zones are meaningfully distant
realWorld.text: AWS's fault isolation guide says Availability Zones in a Region are "meaningfully distant from each other, up to 60 miles (~100 km) to prevent correlated failures", and are "designed not to be simultaneously impacted by a shared fate scenario like utility power, water disruption, fiber isolation, earthquakes, fires, tornadoes, or floods."

realWorld.title: AWS: regions are isolated, and don't copy for you
realWorld.text: The Amazon EC2 guide: "Regions are separate geographic areas." "Each Region is designed to be isolated from the other Regions." And: "Regions are isolated from each other, and we don't automatically replicate resources across Regions." A copy in another region is something you set up yourself. The same page warns: "If you host all of your instances in a single location that is affected by a failure, none of your instances would be available."

realWorld.title: GitLab, 1 February 2017: five methods, none working
realWorld.text: GitLab's post on the night of its database outage: "So in other words, out of five backup/replication techniques deployed none are working reliably or set up in the first place."

realWorld.title: GitLab: backups that failed silently
realWorld.text: GitLab's post-mortem, published ten days later. Of the main database backup: "This procedure failed silently because it was using PostgreSQL 9.2, while GitLab.com runs on PostgreSQL 9.6." And: "This means we were never aware of the backups failing, until it was too late." In the end, "the process of both finding and using backups failed completely."

realWorld.title: GitLab: nobody owned the test
realWorld.text: The post-mortem asks "Why was the backup procedure not tested on a regular basis?" and answers "Because there was no ownership, as a result nobody was responsible for testing this procedure." Its improvements include "Automated testing of recovering PostgreSQL database backups" and "Assign an owner for data durability". Its real RPO: data "created between January 31st 17:20 UTC and 23:30 UTC has been lost."

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, A.8.13: information backup
realWorld.text: Annex A control A.8.13 is titled Information backup. The linked guide, a secondary source, describes its purpose as enabling "timely recovery from loss of data" and says "regular testing of backup jobs is essential", with recovery times "measured against backup tests". The control wording itself is in the standard.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, A.8.14: redundancy
realWorld.text: A.8.14 is titled Redundancy of information processing facilities: enough spare capacity in enough places that one failure does not stop the work. The linked page is a secondary guide; the control wording is in the standard.

realWorld.title: SOC 2 A1.2: backups and recovery infrastructure
realWorld.text: SOC 2's availability criterion A1.2 reads: "The entity authorizes, designs, develops or acquires, implements, operates, approves, maintains, and monitors environmental protections, software, data back- up processes, and recovery infrastructure to meet its objectives." One of its points of focus is "Addresses Offsite Storage".

asked: How do you know a backup works?
interview.answer: RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much recent data you can afford to lose: the gap between the last good copy and the failure. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how long you can be down before you're working again. They come from the business, not the engineers: a shop might accept losing an hour of orders and being down for four, a bank much less. They then decide the design: how often to copy, where, and how fast you must be able to restore. For where, I'd ask what each copy protects against. A mirrored disk or a replica protects against one disk or one machine failing, but it copies mistakes instantly and lives in the same place, so it isn't a backup. A backup in another availability zone usually survives a building or a power failure, since zones are kilometres apart with their own power. A copy in another region survives losing a whole area, and regions don't copy for you, so you set it up. I'd also keep older copies for weeks, because a deleted folder is copied faithfully to every place by the next night. As for knowing a backup works: only a restore proves it. I'd restore from the far copy on a schedule onto a fresh machine, check real records, time it against the RTO, and alert every morning if last night's copy didn't arrive. GitLab in 2017 found that of five backup and copy methods, none was working reliably, and nobody owned testing them. A story I'd tell: a stonemason's archive had nightly backups, tested monthly, to a second building 50 metres away. One fire took both buildings, the only other copy was a nine-day-old USB drive, and a family's spelling correction never made it onto the stone.

The plan, and the copies, for being back at work after losing a whole site or area, not just one machine.
One or more data centres with their own power, cooling and network, kilometres from the next zone, so one fire or power cut usually reaches only one.

Keeping copies in two or more availability zones, so losing one zone loses no copy. Two buildings on one site are not two zones.

Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud company, which rents out servers and storage in regions and availability zones around the world.
A company that runs a website where programmers store and share their code. Its January 2017 outage and post-mortem were public.

atWork: Look for backups that live in the same data centre as the system they protect. It is a common pattern: the nightly job runs, the practice restore passes, the dashboard is green, and the copy sits a few metres or a few buildings from the original, inside the reach of one fire, flood or power cut. Check four things. For each system, what are its RPO and RTO, written down, and who agreed them? For each copy, which disaster can't reach it: a dead disk, a deleted folder, a lost building, a lost region? When did anyone last restore from the far copy, onto a fresh machine, and how long did it take against the RTO? And does anything alert you the morning after a copy fails to arrive? Hand-made copies, like a weekly export, need a second person who can make them. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.13 covers information backup, including testing it, and A.8.14 covers redundancy of information processing facilities; if it is pursuing SOC 2, A1.2 expects data backup processes and recovery infrastructure that meet your objectives, with offsite storage as a point of focus. Putting the far copy and a scheduled restore in now saves rework at audit time.

recall.prompt: A small clinic keeps its patient records on a rented server in a data hall. A nightly job copies them to a second server in the room next door, and every practice restore passes. A pipe bursts above both rooms one night and both servers are ruined. The only other copy is a laptop export from three weeks ago. What was wrong with the plan, and how would you set it up again?

keyIdeas.idea: Both copies were within reach of one event, so the backup gave no protection against it
Keep a copy in another availability zone or region, far enough that one disaster can't reach both
Prove the far copy works by restoring from it on a schedule, and know the RPO and RTO it gives

recall.model: Both copies were in the same place, within reach of one event: a burst pipe over two neighbouring rooms is a shared fate, so both copies were ruined together and the practice restores proved nothing about that night. I'd keep the nightly copy next door for quick restores and add a second copy in another region, or at least another availability zone, kilometres away with its own power. Then I'd restore from the far copy on a schedule, every month, time the restore, and write down the recovery point and recovery time it really gives, so the plan's numbers are measured, not hoped.

recall.prompt: A shop's database is lost at 14:00. Its newest surviving backup was taken at 02:00, and the shop is selling again at 20:00. What were its real RPO and RTO?
recall.why: The RPO is the work lost: from the last good copy at 02:00 to the loss at 14:00, 12 hours. The RTO is the time until working again: from 14:00 to 20:00, 6 hours. At Trethowan's, the same sums gave 8 days 7 hours 10 minutes and 63 hours.

recall.prompt: A colleague says: "Our database has a replica on the next rack and we take a snapshot every hour onto the same storage. Our RPO is an hour, so we're covered." What would you ask, and what is missing?

keyIdeas.idea: A replica copies every change, mistakes and deletions included, so it is not a backup
Copies near the original share its fate: one fire, flood or power cut reaches them all
The real RPO depends on the newest copy that survives the disaster, so keep one far away and restore it to prove it

recall.model: A replica is not a backup: it copies every change the moment it happens, deletions and corruption included, so a bad change reaches it too. And both the replica and the hourly snapshots sit in the same building, probably the same room and on the same power, so one fire or one event takes the database and every copy. The hour is only the RPO if a copy survives. I'd ask which disaster each copy survives, then add a far copy in another region or at least another zone, and run a practice restore from it on a schedule to prove it loads and to see the real RPO and RTO.

recall.prompt: Which copy is most likely to survive a fire that destroys the building holding the original server?
options: A mirrored disk inside the same server
An hourly backup to a server in the next building on the same site
A nightly backup in another region, restored on a schedule
A third building on the same site, 50 metres further on
recall.why: Only the far copy is outside the fire's reach. A mirror lives in the same box; buildings on one site share one fire, as OVHcloud's Strasbourg site and Trethowan's backups showed. Restoring it on a schedule proves it is really there.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The far copy works: every night it reaches the other region, and the practice restore passes each month. On a Tuesday in August, at 16:00, our new apprentice deleted the folder of 1990s drawings by mistake. Nobody noticed until Friday. The nightly copies from Wednesday, Thursday and Friday have no folder. The region keeps only the last 3 nights, and building B the same.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Every copy worked. Why can't any of them give the drawings back, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: A backup copies what is there, mistakes included: the deletion went faithfully into every new copy
Keep older copies for weeks or months, not just the last few nights
Notice sooner: check what changed and practise restoring single folders, not just whole archives

coldCase.model: Every copy did its job faithfully: a backup copies whatever is there, so once the folder was gone, Wednesday's, Thursday's and Friday's copies all carried the deletion too, and with only 3 nights kept, the last copy holding the drawings was dropped on Friday. The far copy guards against a fire, not against a mistake. Keep older copies, with retention of weeks of nightly copies and months of weekly ones, so a mistake found late can still be undone. And notice sooner: an alert when a large share of files disappears, a look at what changed each morning, and a practice restore of a single folder now and then, not only the whole archive.
